lines: A brand-new analytics sink starts reading a compacted topic from the very beginning, days after a particular customer was actually deleted.
By the time that sink gets around to reading it, the one marker that ever proved the delete happened has already been cleaned up.
So that customer, gone from the real database for days now, shows right back up in the sink as though nothing ever happened.
Before I show you what compaction actually keeps, work through this with me.
A single delete produces two separate records sharing the exact same key, written one right after the other.
Does a rule that only ever keeps the newest record for a key hang onto both of those, or only the newer one?
answer: Keeping both would mean the rule somehow understands what a delete record means, which isn't how this works at all.
Only the newer record survives, because that keep-the-latest rule never once looks at what a record actually says.

lines: Here's a detail about deletes that connects straight back to something I showed you earlier in this chapter.
A delete's own before value isn't governed by some separate rule just for deletes.
It follows the exact same table-level setting that decides how much of a row an update's own before value carries.
I confirmed that directly, against the real database, rather than just assuming it carries over.
I ran the identical delete twice: once against a table left at its usual setting, and once against the same table switched to capture full rows.
The first time, only the row's own key came through; the second time, the entire row came through instead.
Now here's why soft and hard deletes end up behaving so differently downstream.
Marking a row deleted without removing it is really just another update, so anything watching for recent changes catches it the same way it catches any other edit.
Actually removing the row leaves nothing behind in the table at all, so that same kind of watcher has nothing left to find.
I measured both of those side by side, using one identical query against the real database.
That query caught the row that was only marked deleted, exactly the way it would catch any ordinary edit.
Against the row that was actually removed, that same query came back with absolutely nothing, every single time.
I also tested how a delete actually lands once it reaches a table meant to hold the current state.
I applied one single statement that inserted a new row, updated an existing one, and removed a third, all in the same pass.
Only the row meant to disappear actually disappeared, and neither of the other two rows was touched at all.
Now for the part that actually explains today's hook, measured the exact same careful way.
I modeled the broker's own keep-the-latest rule by hand, since I don't have a real broker in this sandbox to run it against.

A consumer that came back before its window closed still found the marker and removed the row correctly; one that came back after that window found nothing there at all, and kept treating the row as though it still existed.
Put everything from today side by side, and here's the one thread tying all of it together.

A delete's own before value, whether a cursor notices it, how it lands in a table, and whether a late consumer still sees it — every one of those depends entirely on timing or on a setting made somewhere else.
None of it is a single rule; it's four separate windows, and only one of them is ever actually closing on you.
One more question, because today's incident was entirely avoidable.
Nothing stops a team from staying ahead of this race instead of losing it.
What's the one number that a sink's own maximum allowed lag actually needs to stay under?
answer: How long the source database itself keeps old changes around decides how far back a brand-new read can start from, which is a different question entirely.
Once a delete has already become a marker sitting in a compacted topic, the only clock still running against it is that topic's own tombstone retention window.
